detail.question: What does Mill claim about the abilities of women who have ruled as queens or regents?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Mill argues that women who have ruled have shown real ability to govern. He says that, although history presents few reigning queens compared with kings, a far larger share of those queens have shown talent for rule, even though many reigned in difficult periods (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He adds that queens have often been distinguished by qualities opposite to the conventional image of women, being noted for the firmness and vigour of their rule as much as for its intelligence. When regents and viceroys of provinces are included, the list of eminent women rulers becomes very long (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)). He calls it a fact that Queen Elizabeth could rule, though the law would have kept her from the smallest political duties had she not inherited the throne (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

Mill also answers the joke that under queens men govern. He says most great queens were great through their own talents for government and kept supreme direction of affairs in their own hands. If they listened to good advisers, that shows their judgment fitted them for the great questions of government (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)). He cites women governors of the Netherlands, such as Margaret of Austria, who ruled very successfully (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

In a footnote, Mill says that in Hindoo principalities, a woman's rule as legal regent often goes with strong, orderly, prosperous government. He reports this from long official knowledge and calls it, to him, an unexpected fact. He treats it as a very striking example of women's natural capacity for government, given how secluded and uneducated those princesses were (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Note footnote_2_1 to Chapter 3, paragraph 5 (edition-specific)).

He concludes that women of reigning families, who have the same range of interests and freedom of development as men, show no inferiority. Wherever women's capacities for government have been tried, they have been found adequate in that proportion (John Stuart Mill, The Subjection of Women, Chapter 3, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer: Hobbes lists four abuses of speech that correspond to the proper uses of language. The first is the one that leads to self-deception. It happens when men register their thoughts wrongly because the signification (meaning) of their words is inconstant. They then record as their conceptions things they never conceived, and so deceive themselves (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). The other abuses he lists differ. Using words metaphorically, meaning in a sense other than that they were ordained for, deceives others, not oneself (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 4, Abuses Of Speech, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). A related point appears in Chapter 25. Hobbes calls it fallacious to judge the nature of things by the ordinary and inconstant use of words, and he gives the example of confusing commands with counsel because both are phrased as "Do this" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 25, Counsell What, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). detail.answer: Hobbes traces wax candles in Christian practice to pagan processions. In his account, bearing burning torches and candles before the images of the gods was part of the processions of both the Greeks and the Romans (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). Roman emperors later received the same honor. He cites Caligula, who was met with burning torches, and Caracalla, who was received at Alexandria with incense, flowers, and "Dadouchiais" (torches) (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). Then, "in processe of time," devout but ignorant people honored their bishops with the same pomp of wax candles, and also carried them before images of Christ and the Saints in the Church itself. Hobbes says this is how the use of wax candles came in, and that some ancient Councils also established it (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 37 (edition-specific)). He places this within a broader claim that the Church of Rome imitated heathen customs, which he calls "old empty Bottles of Gentilisme" that Roman Church doctors refilled with Christianity (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Wax Candles, And Torches Lighted, paragraph 38 (edition-specific)). He also argues that such worship was left in the Church by not destroying the images when the Gentiles were converted (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part IV, Chapter 45, Painting Of Fancies No Idolatry: Abusing Them To Religious Worship Is, paragraph 32 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says that power, considered as a whole, is twofold: it is either the ability to make a change or the ability to receive one. The first he calls ACTIVE power and the second PASSIVE power (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §2, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). He leaves open whether matter is wholly without active power. He also leaves open whether created spirits alone can have both kinds. He says these questions may be worth considering but that he will not enter into them here. He suggests that God and spirits give us the clearest idea of active power (same passage).

Later he adds that sensible things abundantly supply ideas of passive power, because their qualities are in continual flux. We also have many instances of active power, since whenever a change is observed the mind must collect a power somewhere able to make it (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §4, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Yet bodies do not give us as clear an idea of active power as reflection on the operations of our own minds does. A ball set in motion is rather passive: its motion is "rather a passion than an action in it". When it sets another ball moving, it only transfers motion and does not produce it (same passage).

The terms recur in Chapter 22. The efficacy that produces a new substance or idea is called ACTION in the subject exerting the power. In the subject in which a simple idea is changed or produced, the same efficacy is called PASSION (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 22, §11, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: Why does Mill claim that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated?
detail.premise: Mill claims that people always think only of their own pain when they feel their sense of justice has been violated.

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Mill does not claim this; the passages show him saying nearly the opposite. He takes up the objection that when our sentiment of justice is outraged we think only of the individual case, not of society. He answers that this is "no objection" to his doctrine (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He grants that it is common, though not commendable, to resent something merely because we have suffered pain. But a person whose resentment is a real moral feeling first considers whether the act is blameable. Even if that person does not say so explicitly, he feels he is asserting a rule that benefits others as well as himself (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). If someone regards the act solely as it affects him individually, Mill says he is not consciously just and is not concerned with the justice of his actions (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)).

Mill's wider account explains why. The raw feeling of retaliation, in itself, has nothing moral in it. It becomes moral only when subordinated to the social sympathies, so that it acts only in directions conforming to the general good (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). He describes the sentiment of justice as the animal desire to repel or retaliate a hurt to oneself or to those one sympathizes with. This desire is widened to include all persons through enlarged sympathy and intelligent self-interest, and from these elements the feeling derives its morality (Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 5, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).

So the passages support only a qualified point. Resentment from one's own pain is common but not moral justice, and genuine justice involves a rule meant for others' benefit too. They do not support the claim that people always think only of their own pain.

detail.question: How does Hobbes distinguish between justice in people and justice in actions?

expected.author: Thomas Hobbes
expected.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Thomas Hobbes
top_retrieved.locator: Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: Hobbes says the names Just and Unjust mean one thing when applied to men and another when applied to actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Applied to men, they signify conformity or inconformity of manners to reason. Applied to actions, they signify conformity or inconformity to reason not of a manner of life but of particular actions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). A just man is one who takes all the care he can that his actions may all be just, and an unjust man is one who neglects this. Such men are more often called Righteous and Unrighteous, though the meaning is the same (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). As a result, a righteous man does not lose that title through one or a few unjust actions that come from sudden passion or mistakes about things or persons. An unrighteous man does not lose his character through actions he does or avoids out of fear, because his will is framed by the apparent benefit of what he is to do, not by justice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). Hobbes says the justice of manners is what is meant when justice is called a virtue and injustice a vice (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part I, Chapter 15, Justice Of Men, And Justice Of Actions What, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke wants his countrymen to hold up the British Constitution as an example for the French to follow, rather than take French models for improving their own. He calls the Constitution "an invaluable treasure" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)). He credits the happy situation of Britain to the whole Constitution, not to any single part. In his view, that owes much to what was left standing in earlier reviews and reformations, as well as to what was altered or added (same passage).

He thinks the English people will find enough to do in guarding what they possess from violation. He does not rule out alteration, but says that even when he changed something, it should be "to preserve." Any remedy should be prompted by a great grievance and should follow the example of the ancestors, repairing "as nearly as possible in the style of the building." He urges imitating the ancestors' caution, since they acted from a sense of human ignorance and fallibility. His summary is: add if we please, but preserve what they left, and be content to admire rather than follow "the aëronauts of France" in their "desperate flights" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 417 (edition-specific)).

He also wants the true principles of Britain's own domestic laws recalled and cherished. He warns against the contempt for ancient institutions and the "spirit of change" that has gone abroad. He also warns against counterfeit doctrines that are passed off as British but are really alien to British soil (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

On French reform, he says abuses in France did need reform. The question, he argues, was whether the old government was so incapable of reform that it had to be entirely pulled down (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 227 (edition-specific)). In his Army Estimates speech, he criticizes the French for glorying in revolution and says they should have secured their existing good constitution and redressed grievances (Edmund Burke, Substance of Speech on the Army Estimates, Volume III, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke says the preacher (Dr. Price, addressing the Revolution Society) claims the king is "almost the only lawful king in the world, because the only one who owes his crown to the choice of his people." Burke tells the British that this is a domestic concern for them: they should seriously consider how solid the only principle is on which these gentlemen acknowledge a king of Great Britain to be entitled to allegiance (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 21 (edition-specific)). Other kings may worry about their own position, but this doctrine "affect[s] our Constitution in its vital parts" (same passage).

Burke's reasons are as follows. First, he argues that the doctrine, applied to the present king, is either nonsense or a "most unfounded, dangerous, illegal, and unconstitutional position." The king does not owe his crown to popular election, so by this rule he is no better than the usurpers who rule elsewhere (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). Second, he suspects a strategy: the propagators hope the abstract principle that popular choice is necessary will be overlooked while the king is not affected, so that audiences grow used to it as an undisputed first principle and it is kept in store for future use. Meanwhile the government is flattered with a reservation in its favor that it has no claim to, and the security it shares with all governments, so far as opinion is security, is taken away (same paragraph 22). Third, Burke says the preachers cannot escape through evasion. If they claim only that some predecessors were chosen in some way, their idea of election no longer differs from inheritance. Whatever the origin of dynasties, the king holds the crown by a fixed rule of succession under the laws of his country (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). He adds that the explicit declaration of a right in the people to choose cannot be evaded (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). Fourth, he warns of the consequences: if no throne but an elective one is lawful, then no act of earlier princes is valid. That would stain the throne with continual usurpation and call into question the statute law passed under earlier kings, such as the Petition of Right and Habeas Corpus (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 43 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: How does Mill distinguish between types of government interference in trade?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Mill separates kinds of interference with trade mainly by asking whether the principle of individual liberty is actually at stake.

1. Trade is a social act, so in principle it falls under society's jurisdiction. Restrictions on trade or on production for trade are "restraints," and all restraint as such is an evil. But they touch only the part of conduct that society is competent to restrain, and they are wrong solely because they fail to produce the results intended. This is the doctrine of Free Trade, which Mill says rests on grounds different from, though equally solid with, the principle of liberty (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

2. Many questions about the limits of free trade do not involve liberty either, such as public control to prevent fraud by adulteration, sanitary precautions, and protecting workers in dangerous occupations. They involve liberty only in the sense that leaving people alone is, other things equal, better than controlling them. Mill says that they may legitimately be controlled for these ends is "in principle undeniable" (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

3. Other interferences with trade are "essentially questions of liberty." Examples are the Maine Law, the prohibition of opium importation into China, and restricting the sale of poisons. In these the aim is to make a commodity impossible or difficult to obtain. They are objectionable not as infringements on the liberty of the producer or seller but on that of the buyer (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

4. Mill also sets aside a further class of questions, which concern helping people rather than restraining them. There the issue is whether government should do something for individuals' benefit instead of leaving it to them or to voluntary combination. The reasons against interference here do not turn on liberty (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 16 (edition-specific)). Interference of this kind can still be objected to, in three ways (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 17 (edition-specific)). The first is when individuals would do the thing better than government. Mill says this principle condemns the once-common interferences by the legislature with the ordinary processes of industry (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 18 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give the second and third objections, so I cannot report them.

detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match what Burke says in these passages. He does not argue that the paper currency scheme will distribute power equally among citizens. He argues the opposite: that it will concentrate power in a few hands. He says the one certain effect of the scheme is "producing an oligarchy in every one of the republics" (an oligarchy is rule by a small group). The paper circulation is not backed by any real money deposited, and it has been forced in place of the kingdom's coin. As a result, whatever power, authority and influence remains must go into "the hands of the managers and conductors of this circulation" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 331 (edition-specific)).

The passages do speak of putting people on an equal footing, but in a critical sense. Burke says the Assembly wished "to put every individual on the same bottom" and to bind the nation in "one guilty interest" to uphold the seizure of Church property. It made its paper circulation compulsory so that even the most reluctant would take part in the pillage (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 220 (edition-specific)). So any equality here is a shared complicity that secures the rulers' power, not an equal distribution of power. Burke also calls the compulsory paper currency a violent outrage upon "credit, property, and liberty" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 221 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not contain any Burke argument for equal distribution of power through the currency. The Adam Smith passages concern the risks of paper money generally and do not address this question.

detail.question: According to Mill, should society always punish individuals for personal failings such as imprudence or lack of dignity?
detail.premise: Mill believes society should punish individuals for personal failings even when these do not harm others.

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
No. Mill holds that society should not punish purely self-regarding failings such as imprudence or lack of personal dignity, though he allows some qualifications.

**The main principle.** Mill distinguishes the loss of consideration a person may rightly incur through "defect of prudence or of personal dignity" from the reprobation (strong condemnation) due to an offence against others' rights (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). For merely self-regarding faults, we may express distaste and keep our distance. But we should not try to make the person's life uncomfortable. Since he already bears the penalty of his error, we should try to ease it rather than add to it (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). The worst we think ourselves justified in doing is leaving him to himself (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)). By contrast, when someone infringes the rules protecting others, society must inflict punishment on him (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 7 (edition-specific)).

Mill restates this as a maxim. The individual is not accountable to society for actions that concern only himself. Society may respond only with advice, instruction, persuasion, and avoidance. Punishment, social or legal, is for actions prejudicial to others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 5, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

**Objections he answers.** Mill anticipates the argument that society should protect mature but unfit persons as it protects children, and should repress vices like gambling, drunkenness, idleness, and uncleanliness (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)). He also anticipates the argument that no one is isolated, so self-harm reaches others (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 8 (edition-specific)). He replies that the merely contingent or "constructive" injury to society from such conduct is an inconvenience society can afford to bear for the greater good of human freedom (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Society has had the whole of childhood to train its members, and if many grow up incapable of rational conduct, it has itself to blame (Mill, On Liberty, Chapter 4, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). expected.locator: Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)

detail.answer:
Locke argues that conquest is not a way of establishing government, and that government rests on consent. The passages leave some details of his full account of conquest unaddressed (for example, what a just conqueror may rightfully claim beyond what is quoted here).

1. Consent is the original basis of government. Locke says governments can originally arise only from the consent of the people. He says many people have mistaken "the force of arms for the consent of the people" and counted conquest as an origin of government (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He compares conquest to demolishing a house, which is not the same as building a new one. Conquest may often make way for a new frame of commonwealth by destroying the old one, but without the people's consent it can never erect a new one (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §175, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

2. Earlier in the work he sets conquest aside. He concludes that all peaceful beginnings of government were laid in the people's consent. He calls them "peaceful" because he will speak of conquest separately, "which some esteem a way of beginning of governments" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §112, paragraph 22 (edition-specific)). He also says the governments of the world that began in peace were made by the consent of the people (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 8, §104, paragraph 13 (edition-specific)). He warns that if government were only the product of force and violence, it would lay a foundation for perpetual disorder (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 1, §1, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

3. A conqueror's power is limited. He gets no power over those who conquered alongside him. Using the Norman conquest of England as an example, Locke says that even if William had a right to make war, his dominion by conquest could reach no further than the Saxons and Britons then living in the country (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §177, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Force alone gives a conqueror only the title that bare force gives the stronger over the weaker. By that reasoning, whoever is strongest would have a right to whatever he pleases to seize (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §184, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)). Even if a just conqueror did have a right to the conquered people's estates (which Locke says he does not), no absolute power would follow. Property is such that it cannot be taken without the owner's consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 16, §193, paragraph 20 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke argues that the French ministers are caught in a position that is both perilous and degrading, for several reasons drawn from his Reflections.

1. Their office has no honor or glory. In other countries the office of minister of state is of the highest dignity, but in France Burke calls it "full of peril, and incapable of glory" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)). He also says the French constitution lets their rivals attack them in their vital parts, while the ministers can answer only in the degrading character of culprits. He adds that they are the only people in France incapable of a share in the national councils (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

2. Responsibility without power. Burke says responsibility prevents crimes but cannot supply "active and zealous service"; the elevation of mind derived from fear will never make a nation glorious (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 350 (edition-specific)).

3. A divided, powerless servitude. Burke describes them as in "a species of subordinate servitude" never before seen. They lack the confidence of the sovereign on whom they were forced, and of the Assembly that forced them upon him. The noble functions of their office are carried out by committees of the Assembly, regardless of their authority. They must "execute, without power," be "responsible, without discretion," and "deliberate, without choice." Serving two sovereigns over neither of whom they have influence, they must sometimes betray one, sometimes the other, and always themselves (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

4. Witnessing their country's degradation. Burke says that, placed on "an eminence of humiliation," they must have felt the evils produced by the Revolution and their utter incapacity to serve their country. He is astonished they have not resigned long since, and says the same situation awaits their successors (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

Burke also supposes that the ministers wished the Revolution well, but he qualifies this with "Let this fact be as it may" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 353 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says that someone who thinks for himself and seeks truth gets real satisfaction from the search, whether or not he finds much. In the Epistle to the Reader he compares the understanding to the eye: it "cannot but be pleased with what it discovers." A person who has "raised himself above the alms-basket" (that is, who no longer lives on scraps of begged opinions) and sets his own thoughts to work will "not miss the hunter's satisfaction." Every moment of the pursuit rewards his pains with some delight, and he has reason to think his time well spent even if he cannot boast of any great acquisition (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)).

Locke also says there is pleasure in knowledge in general. He adds that this pleasure does not move every person's desire. Only goods that a person counts as part of his own happiness do that, and one man may place his satisfaction in sensual pleasures and another in the delight of knowledge (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §44, paragraph 43 (edition-specific)).

Locke also ties satisfaction to knowing the limits of our understanding. If people knew those limits, they would perhaps accept ignorance of what lies beyond them and use their thoughts with more advantage and satisfaction on what lies within them. He says this tentatively ("perhaps") (John Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1 / MDCXC, Based on the 2nd Edition, Books 1 and 2, Volume 1, Book I, Chapter 1, §7, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The question's premise does not match the passages. Locke does not argue that private property is never justified, even in the earliest societies. He argues the opposite: property can arise legitimately, even from a starting point of common ownership. The passages do not contain any argument that property is unjustified.

Locke starts from the view that God gave the earth to mankind in common, and he says this makes it seem difficult to explain how anyone could come to have a property in anything (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says he will try to show how men might come to have property in parts of the common stock without any express compact of all the commoners (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §25, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)).

His answer is labour. Though the things of nature are given in common, a man is master of himself and proprietor of his own person and its labour, so he had in himself the great foundation of property (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §44, paragraph 23 (edition-specific)). Labour in the beginning gave a right of property wherever someone employed it on what was common (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)). For example, a deer becomes the goods of the person who bestowed labour on it, though it was previously the common right of everyone (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §30, paragraph 6 (edition-specific)).

Locke also holds that this early appropriation was not unjust to others. Labour and enjoyment are limited, so no one could take everything. It was therefore impossible for one man to intrench upon another's right, because enough as good was left for others (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §36, paragraph 12 (edition-specific)).

Later, communities settled the bounds of their territories and regulated private property by laws and agreement, building on the property that labour and industry began (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 5, §45, paragraph 24 (edition-specific)).

Locke also treats property as something government must protect. Men join society for the mutual preservation of their lives, liberties and estates, which he calls by the general name property (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 9, §123, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The supreme power cannot take any part of a man's property without his consent (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 11, §138, paragraph 11 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Locke says he is willing to revise his views on liberty when he finds good reason, and that he has already done so. In the chapter on Power he says he gave an account of his thoughts on will, volition, liberty and necessity in an earlier edition, "according to the light I then had." He now describes himself as "a lover of truth, and not a worshipper of my own doctrines," and owns some change of opinion, for which he thinks he has found ground (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78 (edition-specific)). He claims neither infallibility nor a wish to hide his mistakes to protect his reputation. He is therefore not ashamed to publish what a "severer inquiry" suggested, and he expects readers to differ on whether his old or new notions are right. He would be grateful to anyone who could clear the subject of remaining difficulties (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §74, paragraph 78 (edition-specific)).

He explains how the revision came about. He himself feared the earlier treatment of liberty had a mistake, and a judicious friend suspected one but could not show it. This led him to a stricter review of the chapter, where he found a slip: he had put one seemingly indifferent word for another. That discovery gave him the new view he offers in the second edition (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, Book II, Chapter 21, §73, paragraph 77 (edition-specific)).

In the Epistle to the Reader he says he found reason "somewhat to alter" his earlier thoughts about what gives the last determination to the Will in voluntary actions. He acknowledges this as freely as he first published what then seemed right, and he says he is more concerned to renounce an opinion of his own than to oppose another's when truth appears against it. He adds that it is truth alone he seeks (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)).

There is a limit to this readiness. Despite his willingness to give up an opinion on the first evidence of error, he says he has gained no light from the printed objections to his book, and has found no reason to alter his sense of any questioned point (Locke, An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding, Volume 1, THE EPISTLE TO THE READER, paragraph 10 (edition-specific)). That remark is about his book in general rather than about liberty specifically.

detail.answer:
Hobbes says the word 'Church' (Greek Ecclesia) has several meanings in scripture. (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific))

1. A house or temple. Sometimes, though not often, it means God's House, a temple where Christians gather for public holy duties, as in 1 Cor. 14:34. Hobbes calls this a metaphor for the congregation assembled there, a use later extended to the building itself to distinguish Christian temples from those of idolaters. (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Church The Lords House, paragraph 1 (edition-specific))

2. An assembly of citizens. When not taken for a house, it means what Ecclesia meant in the Grecian Commonwealths: a congregation or assembly of citizens called forth to hear the magistrate. If called by lawful authority it was a lawful church (Ecclesia Legitima); if stirred up by tumultuous and seditious clamor, it was a confused church. (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 2 (edition-specific))

3. Several further senses. It can mean the men who have a right to be of the Congregation though not actually assembled, that is, the whole multitude of Christians however dispersed (e.g. Acts 8:3, and Christ as Head of the Church). It can mean a certain part of Christians (Col. 4:15) or the Elect only (Eph. 5:27), meaning the Church Triumphant or Church To Come. It can also mean a congregation assembled of professors of Christianity, whether their profession is true or counterfeit (Mat. 18:17). (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part III, Chapter 39, Ecclesia Properly What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific))

4. Hobbes's own definition, in which the Church can be taken as one person. It can be said to will, command, make laws, or act only in this last sense, which he defines as 'A company of men professing Christian Religion, united in the person of one Soveraign; at whose command they ought to assemble, and without whose authority they ought not to assemble.' detail.answer:
The question's premise is the reverse of what these passages show. Hobbes does not argue that the sovereign should never regulate opinions and doctrines. He argues that judging them belongs to the sovereign. (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific)) His reasons are as follows.

1. Actions proceed from opinions. He says that governing opinions well is what governs men's actions well, for the sake of peace and concord. (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific))

2. Truth and peace do not conflict. He grants that in matters of doctrine only truth should matter. But he says a doctrine repugnant to peace cannot be true, just as peace cannot be against the Law of Nature. So regulating doctrine for peace does not offend against truth. (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific))

3. His conclusion is that the sovereign must be judge of opinions and doctrines, or appoint the judges. He calls this necessary to peace, to prevent discord and civil war. (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 18, And Judge Of What Doctrines Are Fit To Be Taught Them, paragraph 9 (edition-specific))

4. Private conscience is a related danger. Hobbes calls the doctrine that whatever a man does against his conscience is sin repugnant to civil society. He says conscience, like judgement, can be erroneous. For a subject, the law is the public conscience, which he has already undertaken to be guided by. Otherwise the commonwealth would be distracted by diverse private consciences, which he calls private opinions, and no one would obey the sovereign beyond what seemed good in his own eyes. (Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 29, Erroneous Conscience, paragraph 7 (edition-specific))

The passages do not give any argument by Hobbes that the sovereign should never regulate opinions. The arguments against such regulation in the other passages are Mill's, not Hobbes's.

detail.answer:
Hobbes treats a crime as a particular kind of sin, so the two terms are not equivalent. A sin is any deviation from the law, and it includes contempt of the lawgiver. This contempt can lie in a deed, in words, in an omission, or even in an intention or purpose to transgress (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). A crime is a sin that consists in committing, by deed or word, what the law forbids, or in omitting what it commands. He concludes that every crime is a sin but not every sin is a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

The dividing line is whether the sin can be shown outwardly. To intend to steal or kill is a sin even if it never appears in word or deed, because God sees thoughts and can charge a man with them. Human accusation, however, has no place until the intention appears in something done or said (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Hobbes backs this with the Greek and Latin words. In his account, the Greek word translated "Sinne" means any swerving from the law, while the words translated "Crime" mean only the sin of which one man may accuse another. The Latin peccatum covers every deviation from the law, while crimen covers only sins that can be made to appear before a Judge, so it does not cover mere intentions (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, A Crime What, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)).

Hobbes also ties the two to different laws. Sin relates to law in general, and crime relates to the civil law. Where law ceases, sin ceases, but the Law of Nature is eternal, so violating covenants, ingratitude, arrogance and similar acts never cease to be sin. When civil law ceases, crimes cease, because only the Law of Nature remains and there is no place for accusation. In that case a man is judged only by his own conscience and cleared by the uprightness of his own intention. So a man whose intention is wrong commits a sin but not a crime (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Where No Civill Law Is, There Is No Crime, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
The passages only partly answer this. They do not directly discuss a sovereign who openly commands a subject to break the law. They do give two related lines of reasoning.

1. Hobbes treats a sovereign's tacit approval of a forbidden act differently from an express command. He says that when the law-maker approves an act by other signs while the law condemns it, there appear to be "two contradictory Lawes". That would excuse the act totally only if men were bound to take notice of the sovereign's approval by means other than what his command expresses (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). Hobbes does not say subjects are bound to do so. I infer that the offender therefore stays guilty before the law-maker, but the passage does not state this in so many words.

2. Even so, the offence is lessened. Because punishments follow both breaking the law and keeping it, the sovereign is "in part a cause of the transgression". He therefore cannot reasonably blame the whole crime on the offender. Hobbes uses the example of dueling (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 27, Tacite Approbation Of The Soveraign, Extenuates, paragraph 36 (edition-specific)). These acts are "lesse Crimes" than ones condemned by both law and law-maker. That is a reduction in guilt, not a removal of it.

3. On releasing someone from an obligation, Hobbes says that when a man may lawfully perform a promise and does not, what absolves him is not the covenant's invalidity but "the Sentence of the Soveraign" (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, Part II, Chapter 20, Wherein Different From A Common-wealth By Institution, paragraph 2 (edition-specific)). By analogy, release from guilt depends on the sovereign's own judgment, not on the subject's circumstances. This is my inference, not something the passage says about guilt.

The passages do not spell out the case of a direct command to break the law, so they cannot settle exactly how Hobbes reasons about it.

detail.question: According to Locke, why does the bond between male and female animals sometimes last beyond mating?

expected.author: John Locke
expected.locator: Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)

top_retrieved.author: Mary Wollstonecraft
top_retrieved.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

detail.answer: Locke says the bond lasts beyond mating because the purpose of the male–female union is "not barely procreation, but the continuation of the species." The union should therefore continue after procreation for as long as the young need nourishment and support, until they can provide for themselves (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). He says the animals differ according to what their young need. Among grass-feeding viviparous animals (those that bear live young), the bond lasts only through the act of copulation, because the mother's teat can nourish the young and the male can contribute nothing (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Among beasts of prey the bond lasts longer, because the mother cannot easily feed herself and her numerous offspring alone, so the male's help is needed (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Birds likewise stay mates until the young can fly and fend for themselves, with some domestic birds excepted where plentiful food excuses the cock (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §79, paragraph 3 (edition-specific)). Where the young can subsist on their own before the next breeding time, the conjugal bond dissolves of itself (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). Locke gives humans a further reason for a longer union. The woman commonly conceives again and bears a new child before the earlier one is independent, which obliges the father to stay with her longer (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)). He states this with some hedging, saying it is "the chief, if not the only reason" (John Locke, Second Treatise of Government, Book II, Chapter 7, §80, paragraph 4 (edition-specific)).

detail.answer:
Burke raises several concerns about how the confiscated Church lands are being managed financially. He does not give a full accounting, and some figures he admits he cannot ascertain.

1. The fund is burdened with new charges. The Assembly meant the fund to show a surplus free of all charges, but it has loaded it with compensation for the disbanded judicature and for suppressed offices and estates. Burke says he cannot ascertain this sum, but it "unquestionably amounts to many French millions." It is also charged with an annuity of 480,000 pounds sterling for interest on the first assignats (the Assembly's paper currency), payable "if they choose to keep faith" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

2. The cost of management has not been fairly stated. Burke asks whether the Assembly has ever stated the expense of managing the lands through the municipalities and their "legion of unknown under-agents" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 406 (edition-specific)).

3. A sudden mass sale would have defeated the profits. Putting this "unwieldy mass" of land on the market at once would depreciate those lands and all landed estates in France. It would also divert circulating money from trade to land. The Assembly then moved through other schemes, such as exchanging the lands for stock, and in the end admitted the municipalities to a share (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 219 (edition-specific)).

4. The sale terms favor purchasers without money. Only part of the price is paid up front, with twelve years allowed for the rest. Burke calls this "a sort of gift" and says it lets in "a body of purchasers without money." He expects them to pay from rents, from stripping buildings, from waste in woods, and from extortion on the peasants, rather than the state receiving the revenue (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 222 (edition-specific)).

5. The scheme destroys the state's settled revenue and its credit. Burke says only desperate adventurers in philosophy and finance would destroy "the settled revenue of the state, the sole security for the public credit," hoping to rebuild it from confiscated property. He argues that those who took on the role of financier of confiscation were bound to make their bank "a real fund of credit" (Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 401 (edition-specific)).

detail.question: What misconception about the meaning of 'utility' does Mill address in this paragraph?

expected.author: John Stuart Mill
expected.locator: Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)

detail.answer: In Chapter 2, paragraph 1, Mill addresses the mistaken idea that utilitarians use "utility" in a narrow, everyday sense in which it is opposed to pleasure. He calls this an "ignorant blunder" (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He says that writers from Epicurus to Bentham who held the theory of utility meant by it "pleasure itself, together with exemption from pain" (that is, freedom from pain), not something set apart from pleasure. They also declared that the useful includes the agreeable and the ornamental, among other things (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He notes that the misunderstanding is odd because utilitarianism is also commonly accused of the opposite fault, of reducing everything to pleasure in its grossest form. The same people often make both charges (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). He adds that people who know only the sound of the word "utilitarian" use it to mean rejection or neglect of pleasure, beauty, ornament or amusement. Sometimes they use it as a compliment, as if it implied superiority to frivolity (John Stuart Mill, Utilitarianism, Chapter 2, paragraph 1 (edition-specific)). The passage as given is cut off mid-sentence, so I cannot report how Mill finishes his point.

detail.answer:
Burke gives several connected reasons for disliking the constant talk of resistance and revolution.

1. It turns an emergency remedy into a daily habit. He says he never liked "this continual talk of resistance and revolution, or the practice of making the extreme medicine of the Constitution its daily bread." He argues that this makes the habit of society "dangerously valetudinary" (that is, sickly and prone to invalidism). He compares it to taking periodic doses of poison or provocatives to our love of liberty. He also fears that the anniversary sermons commemorating the Revolution will "cheat many out of the principles" and the benefits of the Revolution they celebrate (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 112 (edition-specific)).

2. It damages moral sentiments for no political gain. Burke says revolutionary politics "temper and harden the breast" for desperate strokes that are sometimes used on extreme occasions. Those occasions may never arrive, so the mind takes on a "gratuitous taint" and morals suffer when no political purpose is served. He adds that such people are so taken up with the rights of man that they have forgotten his nature (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 114 (edition-specific)).

3. It encourages contempt for ancient institutions and a spirit of change. He dislikes revolutions whose signals are so often given from pulpits. He also dislikes the contempt for ancient institutions, set against "a present sense of convenience" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 46 (edition-specific)).

4. It misreads the settlement of 1688. Burke says the caution of that settlement shows the aim was to make the Revolution "a parent of settlement, and not a nursery of future revolutions." The point is that men elevated by a triumph over oppression are apt to abandon themselves to violent and extreme courses (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 49 (edition-specific)).

The passages do not give a fuller account of why the habit of celebration itself is harmful beyond these points.

detail.answer:
Burke argues that, under the new French Constitution, the people and their representatives are almost disconnected. He says there is "little, or rather no, connection between the last representative and the first constituent." A member of the National Assembly "is not chosen by the people, nor accountable to them." Three elections come before he is chosen, and two sets of magistracy stand between him and the primary assembly. This makes him "an ambassador of a state, and not the representative of the people within a state" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke thinks this cannot easily be fixed. If primary electors tried to bind the later electors with instructions, it would subvert the scheme and bring back the "tumult and confusion of popular election" the gradation was meant to avoid. He concludes that unless the people break up this gradation, they do not substantially elect to the Assembly at all, and "they elect as little in appearance as reality" (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 326 (edition-specific)).

Burke also contrasts this with Britain. In France the elective Assembly is the sole sovereign, and its members are integral parts of that sovereignty. In Britain a representative, separated from the other parts of government, "can have no action and no existence." There, the government is the point of reference for the representation and acts as a trustee for the whole, not for the parts (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 325 (edition-specific)). He says the French treat the National Assembly as a general congress of ambassadors from independent republics, tied together only by their acquiescence (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 318 (edition-specific)).

Burke further argues that numbers alone do not justify this arrangement. The will and the interest of the many often differ, and he says a government of five hundred country attorneys and obscure curates would not be good for twenty-four millions of men even if chosen by eight-and-forty millions (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 93 (edition-specific)). He predicts that France would end up governed by an "ignoble oligarchy" founded on the destruction of the people among others (Edmund Burke, Reflections on the Revolution in France, Volume III, REFLECTIONS ON THE REVOLUTION IN FRANCE., paragraph 339 (edition-specific)). The passages give his claims as his own judgments and predictions, not as settled outcomes.
